newsitem.title: UAE: Gulf Arabs say differ with U.S. attacks on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arabs say differ with U.S. attacks on Iraq.

text.p: Gulf Arab states differ with the United States over its attacks on Iraq and are discussing the issue with their main Western ally, a Gulf minister said on Sunday.

"...There are no disagreements but there are differences in opinion," Oman's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Youssef bin Alawi bin Abdullah said when asked if Gulf states disagreed with Washington over its missile attacks on Iraq last week.

His comments, at the end of a two-day meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh, were the first public word on the Gulf Arabs' differences with the United States over its strikes on Iraq.

Abdullah said the GCC "totally supports the international coalition...As for the steps and differences that followed the latest U.S. military operations in Iraq, those are at the centre of discussions between a number of coalition countries."
He said discussions between the GCC members "and the U.S. are continuing in a positive manner."

Diplomats said most of the Gulf states felt the U.S. strikes on Iraq, which Washington said were a response to the Iraqi army's intervention in northern Iraq to help a Kurdish faction fighting a rival group, were unjustified since Iraq's action was an internal matter and not a threat to its neighbours.
Much of the Arab world has condemned the attacks as infringing on Iraq's sovereignty. Of the Gulf states only Kuwait had said it fully undertood the U.S. action.
A statement issued after the foreign ministers' talks earlier on Sunday made no mention of the U.S. attacks and the Omani minister said the group felt "there was no need" for that.

The GCC's Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates are part of the U.S.-led coalition that ended Iraq's 1990-91 occupation of Kuwait and supported further U.S. action against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

The GCC ministers asserted in their statement "the importance of a unified political stand by the countries of the international coalition" and renewed support "for all efforts and measures taken by the countries of the international coalition to ensure Iraq's adherence to total and precise implementation of all Security Council resolutions."

The statement said the GCC states were "greatly concerned" with "the grave developments in northern Iraq" and "strongly condemn the interference of some neighbouring countries in northern Iraq and calls on these countries to immediately and completely halt the interference in Iraq's internal affairs."
It was apparently referring to reported Iranian support for one of the Kurdish groups in Iraq and Turkey's plans to set up a security zone across the Iraqi border.
Abdullah said the GCC opposed Turkey's security zone plans, which Ankara says aim to root out Kurdish rebels fighting for self-rule in southeast Turkey.
He also said the GCC supported an extended no-fly zone over Iraq. The United States uses planes from warships in the Gulf and facilities in Saudi Arabia to enforce the zone.

The GCC urged Iraq to cooperate with the United Nations to provide the appropriate circumstances to speed up the implementation of resolution 986, referring to the decision which would allow Iraq to sell limited amounts of oil for food.
It also stressed the need to preserve Iraq's independence and sovereignty, territorial unity and its regional peace.
